title: Verbalized Bayesian Persuasion
one_liner: Extend Bayesian persuasion from numeric toy settings to dialogue settings by letting language agents send messages while a game solver checks the strategic constraints.
lead: Bayesian persuasion asks how a sender should reveal information to influence a receiver's action. Classic treatments usually write the whole problem in numbers, which makes the math clean but limits the range of situations that can be studied. This paper moves the setting into dialogue. It lets language agents play the sender and receiver, while a solver enforces the strategic rules needed for persuasion to remain well defined.

problem.h2: Why classic persuasion models stop at toy settings
paras: Information design begins with ordinary communication. A recommender, a public official, or a diplomat chooses what to say because that message can shift someone else's action. Classic persuasion theory studies this effect carefully, but it often encodes states, signals, and actions in small numeric games.

That abstraction is useful for theory, yet it leaves a gap when the interaction is an actual conversation. Real dialogue includes wording choices, partial disclosure, and multi-stage exchanges. The paper asks whether strategic persuasion can be studied in language without losing the formal structure of the original game.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Map Bayesian persuasion into a mediator-augmented dialogue game where language agents speak, while a game solver checks commitment and obedience constraints behind the scenes.

panels.title: 1. A sender knows more than a receiver
panels.viz_args: The sender wants the receiver to take a favorable action
panels.caption: The sender cannot directly choose the action, so the only lever is the message.

panels.title: 2. A plain language exchange is hard to analyze
panels.viz_args: Words are flexible and the state is hidden
panels.caption: Without a formal structure, it is hard to tell whether a persuasion strategy is truly sound.

panels.title: 3. Insert a strategic scaffold
panels.caption: The solver keeps the strategic rules visible while the language agents supply the dialogue.

panels.title: 4. Search for a better persuasion policy
panels.viz_args: The algorithm combines language generation with equilibrium finding
panels.caption: A good message policy must help the sender while still giving the receiver a reason to follow the recommendation.

panels.title: 5. The framework handles richer dialogue games
panels.caption: The result is a persuasion model that can operate in recommendation, law, and diplomacy scenarios.

steps.text: Represent the sender, receiver, hidden state, and possible actions in a setting where messages are written in language.

steps.b: Use language agents for the dialogue
steps.text: Let one agent play the sender and another play the receiver so that the interaction can express richer strategies than a small signal table.
Use a solver to enforce commitment and obedience conditions because strategic persuasion requires those constraints to remain valid.

Iteratively improve the sender's language strategy while checking whether the receiver would still follow it, because a persuasive message is only useful when it changes action without breaking obedience.
Evaluate the framework on recommendation, law-enforcement, and diplomacy tasks where the state and messages both affect the final action in a concrete way.

paras: The paper changes the form of Bayesian persuasion. Instead of a small numeric signaling scheme, the sender's policy becomes a language policy that is still anchored by formal strategic constraints.
object.object: the sender's information-revelation policy in a dialogue game

hidden.name: how much of the true state should be revealed in language
paras: The central hidden quantity is the message policy over the true state. The sender knows the state, but the best message is rarely full disclosure or full concealment. The sender needs the right amount and style of revelation to guide the receiver toward the preferred action.

That choice is hard in dialogue because wording matters. The framework handles this by keeping the strategic side explicit. The solver checks whether the receiver still has a reason to obey, so the language policy is optimized within the same logic that classical persuasion uses.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the strategic choices that determine whether a language message changes the receiver's action in the intended way.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is how the sender should describe the situation so that the receiver chooses the desired action.
The method lifts the persuasion signal from a numeric object to a language policy while preserving the commitment and obedience structure that defines Bayesian persuasion.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: let language express the strategy while the solver protects the game
paras: A pure dialogue system can generate persuasive messages, but it may ignore whether those messages fit the strategic assumptions of the game. A pure game solver can enforce the assumptions, but it cannot represent varied language acts. The paper combines them so that each part does what it is good at.

That combination helps because the language agent can explore nuanced messages while the solver rejects policies that break commitment or obedience. In this way, the framework can handle real dialogue scenarios without giving up the formal discipline that makes persuasion theory useful.

stages.s: A hidden state and a dialogue persuasion objective
Generate sender and receiver messages in language
Check strategic constraints with a solver
Update the sender policy toward stronger valid messages because only messages that preserve obedience can be used safely in the next round
A persuasion policy that works in dialogue because it stays strategically valid

math.h2: Choose the message policy that helps the sender while preserving obedience
math.words: A compact summary is to maximize the sender's expected payoff over message policies, subject to the condition that the receiver still prefers to follow the recommended action after hearing the message.
math.equation: best_policy = argmax_policy sender_payoff(policy) subject to obedience(policy)
symbols: the sender message policy that the framework is searching for
the sender's expected payoff under that message policy
the condition that the receiver still wants to follow the recommendation
a rule that maps the hidden state to a language message

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Policy A always gives the same vague message, so the receiver learns little and often ignores the recommendation.
Its sender payoff is low because the receiver's action rarely changes in the desired direction.
Policy B reveals the right evidence for each state while keeping the recommendation believable.
Its sender payoff is higher because the receiver now has a reason to follow the suggested action.
The framework prefers Policy B because it improves the sender's objective without breaking obedience.

math.note: The paper solves a broader equilibrium problem, but this statement captures the central idea that persuasive messages must both help the sender and remain followable for the receiver because the receiver must still prefer the recommended action after hearing the message.

charts.title: Plain dialogue without strategic checking
charts.note: Free-form dialogue alone is weak because it can produce persuasive-sounding messages that do not hold up under the game constraints.

charts.title: Verbalized Bayesian persuasion
charts.note: The paper reports stronger strategies because the language policy is searched together with the formal strategic checks.

items.html: A solver can check strategic conditions, but the quality of the message wording may still vary in ways that are hard to score automatically.

items.b: Real people may react differently from the modeled receiver.
items.html: A persuasion policy that works for the receiver model may fail with humans because real judgments and trust patterns can differ.
As the number of stages increases, the search over valid message policies can become harder because future reactions depend on earlier wording choices.
The framework matters because it brings persuasion theory into dialogue without abandoning the strategic constraints that define the problem.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small persuasion environment with one sender, one receiver, and a hidden state, then run it in natural-language settings such as recommendation letters or public statements. Compare plain language prompting against a verbalized-persuasion system that also checks commitment and obedience with a solver.

The demo should log the hidden state, the produced message, the receiver's action, and whether the strategic constraints were satisfied. The solver-guided system should achieve a better sender payoff because it searches only among message policies that the receiver still has reason to follow.
demo.metric_eq: persuasion_gain = sender_payoff_framework - sender_payoff_plain ; obedience_rate = valid_dialogues / total_dialogues
demo.closing: The result should show that dialogue persuasion becomes more useful when language generation is tied to explicit game constraints.
